title: How to Choose a Standing Desk for Your Home Office
excerpt: Setting up a home office for the first time? Here is a practical checklist for choosing a standing desk, plus simple tips for using it comfortably day to day.
meta_description: A friendly checklist for choosing a standing desk for your home office: height range, stability, motor, size, cables, warranty, and how to use it well.
body_html:
If you are setting up a home office for the first time, a standing desk can look like a big decision. There are lots of options, and the specifications are not always easy to read. This guide walks through what to check before you buy, and how to get the most from the desk once it arrives.

Why consider a standing desk at all?

A standing desk lets you change position during the day instead of staying in one posture for hours. Good ergonomics is mostly about variety and fit: a desk, chair and screen set up so your body is relaxed and supported. A height-adjustable desk makes that fit much easier to achieve, because you can fine-tune it rather than making do with a fixed surface.

What to check before you buy

1. Height range

This is the most important number on the product page. The desk needs to go low enough for you to sit with your elbows at roughly a right angle, and high enough for comfortable standing. Taller and shorter people often find a fixed-height desk awkward, which is where a wide range helps. For example, our desks adjust from 62 cm to 127 cm, which covers a broad span of users. Whatever desk you look at, measure your own seated and standing elbow heights first and compare.

2. Stability

A desk that wobbles when you type is tiring to use. Stability depends on the frame design, the leg construction and how high the desk is raised. Look for a sturdy frame, adjustable feet for uneven floors, and reviews or descriptions that mention how the desk behaves at standing height, not just when lowered.

3. Motor and weight capacity

Electric desks use one or two motors to raise and lower the frame. Dual-motor frames tend to feel smoother and can carry more; ours carry up to 120 kg. Add up what will sit on the desk, such as monitors, a laptop, a printer and a speaker, and leave a comfortable margin. Memory presets are a handy extra, since they let you jump between your sitting and standing heights with one press.

4. Desktop size and shape

Think about what you actually do at your desk. If you use two monitors, write by hand or spread out papers, you will want more depth and width. If your room is small, a compact top may suit you better. Also check that the desktop is thick and solid enough not to flex, and that the edges are comfortable for resting your forearms.

5. Cable management

Because the desk moves, cables need slack and a place to go. Look for a cable tray, clips or channels, and leave enough length so nothing gets pulled or pinched when the desk rises. Tidy cables also make a small home office feel calmer.

6. Warranty and support

An electric desk has moving parts, so warranty terms matter. Check how long the frame and the motors are covered, as they are often different. Ours come with a 5 year warranty on desk frames and a 2 year warranty on motors. Read what is included and how to make a claim before you order.

How to use a standing desk well

Alternate sitting and standing

Standing all day is not the goal. Most people find it works best to switch between positions. Start with short periods of standing, perhaps for part of an hour, and build up gradually as it feels comfortable. If your legs or back feel tired, sit down. An anti-fatigue mat and supportive shoes can help if you stand for longer.

Set your monitor height

  • Place the top of the screen at or just below eye level.
  • Keep it about an arm's length away.
  • Tilt it slightly back so you are not craning your neck.
  • If you use a laptop, consider a separate keyboard and a stand so the screen can sit higher.

Check your arms and wrists

Whether sitting or standing, keep your elbows close to your body and bent at about a right angle, with your wrists in a neutral position. Adjust the desk height until that feels natural, then save it as a preset if your desk has one.

A simple buying checklist

  1. Measure your seated and standing elbow heights.
  2. Choose a height range that covers both with room to spare.
  3. Add up the weight of your equipment and pick a suitable capacity.
  4. Decide on desktop size based on your space and tasks.
  5. Plan your cable routing.
  6. Read the warranty terms for frame and motor.

Final thoughts

You do not need to get everything perfect on day one. Pick a desk that fits your body and your room, set it up carefully, and adjust as you learn what feels good. A well-chosen standing desk can make a new home office more comfortable and flexible for a long time.

faq.question: How tall should my standing desk go?
faq.answer: It should rise high enough that your elbows are bent at about a right angle when you stand with your wrists level. Measure your standing elbow height and compare it with the desk's maximum height before buying.

faq.question: Do I need a dual-motor standing desk?
faq.answer: Not always, but dual-motor frames usually feel smoother and carry heavier loads, with ours supporting up to 120 kg. If you use multiple monitors or heavy equipment, they are worth considering.

faq.question: How long should I stand each day?
faq.answer: There is no single right answer. Most people do best alternating between sitting and standing, starting with short standing periods and building up as it feels comfortable.

faq.question: What warranty should I look for?
faq.answer: Check how long the frame and the motors are covered, since they can differ. Our frames have a 5 year warranty and our motors a 2 year warranty.
